examples.question_text: A grower randomly selects four apples from an unchanged population each morning and records their mean mass. Explain why the sample mean $\bar{X}$ is a random variable while the population mean $\mu$ is fixed. Define the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$.
examples.solution_text:
Different samples can contain different apples and give different means. The value of $\bar{X}$ therefore depends on chance, so it is a random variable.

The population is unchanged, so its mean $\mu$ is fixed.

The sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is the distribution of the means of all possible random samples of size four, together with their probabilities.

examples.question_text: A population consists of the values $2$, $5$ and $8$. Two values are selected independently at random with replacement, and their order is recorded. Write the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$.
examples.solution_text:
There are $3\times3=9$ equally likely ordered samples. Rows show the first selection, columns show the second, and each cell gives the sample mean.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc} &2&5&8\\\hline 2&2&3.5&5\\5&3.5&5&6.5\\8&5&6.5&8\end{array}$

Collecting equal means gives

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}\bar{x}&2&3.5&5&6.5&8\\\hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x})&\frac19&\frac29&\frac39&\frac29&\frac19\end{array}$

Check the total probability:

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{1+2+3+2+1}{9}\\&=1\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A population consists of four objects with values $2$, $4$, $8$ and $10$. Two objects are selected at random without replacement, with every pair equally likely. Write the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$.
examples.solution_text:
List each unordered pair once; repeated selections are excluded.

$\begin{array}{c|cccccc}\text{Sample}&\{2,4\}&\{2,8\}&\{2,10\}&\{4,8\}&\{4,10\}&\{8,10\}\\\hline \bar{x}&3&5&6&6&7&9\end{array}$

Each pair has probability $\frac16$. Two pairs have mean $6$, giving

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}\bar{x}&3&5&6&7&9\\\hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x})&\frac16&\frac16&\frac26&\frac16&\frac16\end{array}$

Check the total probability:

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{1+1+2+1+1}{6}\\&=1\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
The sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ is

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}\bar{x}&15&16&17&18&19\\\hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x})&0.12&0.23&0.30&0.23&0.12\end{array}$

Find the probability that $\bar{X}$ is within $1$ of $17$, including the endpoints.

Two values are selected independently at random with replacement from the population $3$, $6$ and $9$. The sampling distribution is

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}\bar{x}&3&4.5&6&7.5&9\\\hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x})&\frac19&\frac29&\frac39&\frac29&\frac19\end{array}$

Calculate $E(\bar{X})$ from this distribution and compare it with the population mean.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}E(\bar{X})&=3\left(\frac19\right)+4.5\left(\frac29\right)+6\left(\frac39\right)+7.5\left(\frac29\right)+9\left(\frac19\right)\\&=\frac{3+9+18+15+9}{9}\\&=6\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mu&=\frac{3+6+9}{3}\\&=6\end{aligned}$

The sampling distribution has the same mean as the population: $E(\bar{X})=\mu$.

examples.question_text:
A population consists of the four values $2$, $6$, $10$ and $14$.

(a) Three values are selected at random without replacement. Compare the mean and range of $\bar{X}$ with those of the population.

(b) Instead, two values are selected independently at random with replacement. Find the smallest and largest possible sample means, and explain why the sampling distribution differs from the population distribution.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The population mean is

$\begin{aligned}\mu&=\frac{2+6+10+14}{4}\\&=8\end{aligned}$

The four equally likely samples have means $6$, $\frac{22}{3}$, $\frac{26}{3}$ and $10$.

$\begin{aligned}E(\bar{X})&=\frac{6+\frac{22}{3}+\frac{26}{3}+10}{4}\\&=8\end{aligned}$

The population range is $14-2=12$. The sample-mean range is $10-6=4$. The mean is unchanged and the range is smaller.

(b) Selecting $(2,2)$ gives the smallest mean, $2$; selecting $(14,14)$ gives the largest mean, $14$. The sample-mean range remains $12$.

Each extreme mean has probability $\frac{1}{16}$, whereas mean $8$ comes from $(2,14)$, $(6,10)$, $(10,6)$ and $(14,2)$, giving probability $\frac{4}{16}$.

The population values are equally likely, but the sample means are not. The sampling distribution retains mean $8$ and clusters more around it, even though its range is unchanged.

(a) The bars at $8$ and $10$ have probabilities $0.2$ and $0.1$.

$\begin{aligned}P(\bar{X}\ge8)&=0.2+0.1\\&=0.3\end{aligned}$

(b) Read each probability from its bar height.

$\begin{aligned}E(\bar{X})&=2(0.1)+4(0.2)+6(0.4)+8(0.2)+10(0.1)\\&=0.2+0.8+2.4+1.6+1\\&=6\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
Two values are selected independently at random with replacement from a population of three equally likely, distinct values. The sampling distribution is

$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}\bar{x}&4&7&10&13&16\\\hline P(\bar{X}=\bar{x})&\frac19&\frac29&\frac39&\frac29&\frac19\end{array}$

Find the three population values and check that they produce the given distribution.
examples.solution_text:
The smallest possible mean occurs when the smallest population value is selected twice, so that value is $4$. Similarly, the largest population value is $16$.

$\begin{aligned}E(\bar{X})&=\frac{4+2(7)+3(10)+2(13)+16}{9}\\&=\frac{90}{9}\\&=10\end{aligned}$

Let the middle population value be $a$. Since $E(\bar{X})=\mu$,

$\begin{aligned}\frac{4+a+16}{3}&=10\\a+20&=30\\a&=10\end{aligned}$

The population values are $4$, $10$ and $16$. Their nine equally likely ordered samples give these means:

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}&4&10&16\\\hline 4&4&7&10\\10&7&10&13\\16&10&13&16\end{array}$

The frequencies are $1$, $2$, $3$, $2$ and $1$, matching the given probabilities.

examples.derivation: The unchanged population has a fixed mean. Random selection determines the sample and hence its mean. All possible sample means for the fixed size four, with their probabilities, define the sampling distribution.

The nine ordered pairs produce means 2, 3.5, 5; 3.5, 5, 6.5; 5, 6.5, 8. Their frequencies are 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, giving the stated probabilities, which total 1. The bare probability-sum expression has the required phantom gutter.
The six equally likely pairs have means 3, 5, 6, 6, 7, 9. Aggregation gives probabilities 1/6, 1/6, 2/6, 1/6, 1/6, totalling 1. The probability-sum working has the required phantom gutter.
Including endpoints, within 1 of 17 means 16 ≤ X̄ ≤ 18. The required probability is 0.23 + 0.30 + 0.23 = 0.76.
The weighted numerator is 3 + 9 + 18 + 15 + 9 = 54, so E(X̄) = 54/9 = 6. Independently, μ = (3 + 6 + 9)/3 = 6.

For sampling three without replacement, the means are 6, 22/3, 26/3 and 10; their sum is 32 and expected mean is 8. Their range is 4 versus population range 12. With replacement, the extreme means remain 2 and 14, each occurring once among 16 ordered pairs; mean 8 occurs four times. The expected mean remains 8 and the probabilities show central clustering.

The chart assigns probabilities 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2 and 0.1 to sample means 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 respectively; their sum is 1. Thus P(X̄≥8)=0.2+0.1=0.3. Independently, E(X̄)=2×0.1+4×0.2+6×0.4+8×0.2+10×0.1=0.2+0.8+2.4+1.6+1=6. Every bar height agrees with these probabilities. The probability-axis label is now 15.4 mm left of the axis, and the horizontal-axis label is 15.75 mm below it. The explicit bounding box reserves surrounding space. The repair preserves chart values, working, black unshaded marks, 10 pt ordinary labels and 8.5 pt ticks.

Repeated endpoint selections establish population endpoints 4 and 16. The weighted mean is (4 + 14 + 30 + 26 + 16)/9 = 10. Hence (4 + a + 16)/3 = 10 gives a = 10. Enumerating all nine ordered pairs confirms means 4, 7, 10, 13, 16 with frequencies 1, 2, 3, 2, 1.
